claims.text: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a primarily FCC matrix.
Synergy among Al, Cr, and Ti promotes formation of a stable protective oxide at high temperature.
The protective oxide mitigates outward diffusion of Fe and Ni.
The protective oxide limits internal oxidation.
The proposed oxide-forming synergy preserves the FCC matrix during elevated-temperature gas exposure.
The proposed oxide-forming synergy preserves mechanical strength during elevated-temperature gas exposure.
Changing oxygen partial pressure between oxidizing and reducing conditions will affect oxide-scale formation and stability.
Al, Cr, and Ti concurrently partition into a continuous surface oxide scale.
The continuous surface oxide curbs substrate oxidation and phase instability.
Under oxidizing conditions, Al-, Cr-, and Ti-rich oxide phases form preferentially.
The Al-, Cr-, and Ti-rich oxides impede further oxygen ingress.
Under reducing conditions, an oxide-based barrier limits subsurface reaction kinetics.
Under suitable composition and atmosphere, the alloy will exhibit minimal mass gain.
Under suitable composition and atmosphere, the alloy will maintain a uniform oxide scale.
Under suitable composition and atmosphere, the alloy will retain its mechanical properties and resist extensive scaling or phase transformation.
Disrupting the Al-Cr-Ti synergy will cause brittleness, deeper oxidation, or phase breakdown.
The proposed mechanism is applicable up to approximately 1000 °C in both moderately reducing and strongly oxidizing environments.
Systematically varying Al, Cr, and Ti while holding high-temperature exposure conditions constant can test whether those elements govern oxide stability and mechanical integrity.
Failure of Al, Cr, or Ti variation to affect oxide stability or mechanical integrity, or failure of the starting alloy to maintain a protective scale, would invalidate the hypothesis.
